title: Rydberg-mediated Microwave-to-optical Transduction With Tunable Bandwidth
authors: Iason Tsiamis, David Petrosyan, Anders S. S{\o}rensen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coherent microwave-to-optical transduction is essential for hybrid quantum networks. Typical transducers, however, have bandwidths set by fixed device parameters and face efficiency-bandwidth tradeoffs. We propose a cavity-based microwave-to-optical transducer mediated by a collective Rydberg excitation, where external driving fields tune the conversion bandwidth in situ from narrowband, spectrally selective operation to broadband operation without modifying cavity parameters. Under impedance-matching conditions, the system operates as a continuous-wave phase-preserving linear transducer, maintaining both near-unit efficiency and quantum-limited added noise throughout the tunable bandwidth range.
tldr: A cavity-based microwave-to-optical transducer using collective Rydberg excitations can tune its conversion bandwidth in situ while maintaining near-unit efficiency and quantum-limited added noise.
motivation: Coherent microwave-to-optical transduction is essential for hybrid quantum networks, but typical transducers have fixed bandwidths and face efficiency-bandwidth tradeoffs.
method: The authors propose a cavity-based transducer mediated by a collective Rydberg excitation, where external driving fields tune the conversion bandwidth without modifying cavity parameters, operating under impedance-matching conditions as a continuous-wave phase-preserving linear transducer.
result: The system achieves near-unit efficiency and quantum-limited added noise throughout the tunable bandwidth range, from narrowband spectrally selective to broadband operation.
conclusion: This Rydberg-mediated approach enables tunable-bandwidth microwave-to-optical conversion suitable for hybrid quantum networks, overcoming fixed-parameter limitations of conventional transducers.

title: Minimum Experimental Information For Certifying Bell Nonlocality Of Gravity
authors: Jianqi Sheng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03726v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A Bell violation by material probes certifies nonlocal behavior, but it does not identify which internal subsystem carried or was measured to produce that behavior. We determine the additional information required to attribute such a violation to a gravitational field. For any setting-independent field-to-probe channel completed before the Bell settings are chosen, an entanglement-breaking channel makes all induced field measurements jointly measurable. A static Newtonian phase pickup belongs to this class, even with arbitrary adaptive probe control. Applied to a recent four-mass proposal, the claimed field-only measurements obey the stronger CHSH bound \(\sqrt2\), whereas the Bell-active operation is the source-to-probe instrument that includes the coherent source herald. At the published parameters, the observed flagged behavior is at least \(0.1630\) from the claimed field-detector family, exceeding its \(0.0898\) distance from Bell locality. We then incorporate a common field slice, gravitational constraints, dressing, detector backreaction, and coherent references into a robust certification theorem. The result isolates the minimum missing information: field-only factorization and a local measurement- incompatibility witness on each wing. More precise phase data cannot replace either requirement.
tldr: Determines the minimal additional information needed to attribute a Bell violation to a gravitational field, showing that field-only measurements cannot be Bell-active and require a specific certification criterion.
motivation: A Bell violation by material probes certifies nonlocality but does not identify which internal subsystem produced it; attributing such a violation to gravity demands extra experimental or theoretical information.
method: Analyzes setting-independent field-to-probe channels, proves that entanglement-breaking channels make all induced field measurements jointly measurable, applies this to a recent four-mass proposal, and derives a robust certification theorem incorporating field slices, gravitational constraints, dressing, backreaction, and coherent references.
result: Field-only measurements obey the stronger CHSH bound sqrt(2), the Bell-active operation must include the coherent source herald, and at published parameters the observed behavior is at least 0.1630 from the claimed field-detector family versus only 0.0898 from Bell locality.
conclusion: Certifying gravitational Bell nonlocality requires field-only factorization and a local measurement-incompatibility witness on each wing; more precise phase data cannot substitute for either requirement.

title: Multi-Indexed Schatten Quasi- And Anti-Norms And Additivity Of Conditional R\'enyi Entropies
authors: Jan Kochanowski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04023v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce and study multi-indexed Schatten spaces which lift the commutative [MATH] -spaces to the quantum toolbox. They extend Pisier's operator-valued Schatten norms and the recently introduced two-indexed Schatten quasi-norms. For every ordered tuple [MATH] of non-zero indices we define a quasi-norm (for positive indices) or an anti-norm (for negative indices) on operators on an [MATH]-fold tensor product of Hilbert spaces. We do this for indices of the same sign satisfying the mutual compatibility condition [MATH]. Beyond establishing desirable properties of these quasi- and anti-norms via factorization formulas that combine operator space and matrix-analytic techniques, we lift several central tools and results of the seminal [Devetak, Junge, King, Ruskai, CMP 2006] to the multi-indexed and quasi-normed setting. These include a general non-commutative Minkowski inequality relating swapped systems and two identity-removal equalities. As a consequence, complete hypercontractivity and complete reverse hypercontractivity tensorize for all compatible indices, including negative ones. Concerning quantum information theory we prove that the completely bounded minimal and the maximal output conditional entropies are additive under tensor products of quantum channels for all [MATH]. This extends the case [MATH] of [Fawzi, Kochanowski, Rouz\'e, Van Himbeeck, CMP 2026] and the unconditional results of [Devetak, Junge, King, Ruskai, CMP 2006]. Beyond tensor products, we establish chain rules for [MATH], [MATH], for compositions of possibly signaling channels, extending upon the smooth max-entropy chain rule used in device-independent entanglement certification to the whole interval [MATH].
tldr: The paper introduces multi-indexed Schatten quasi- and anti-norms and uses them to prove additivity of completely bounded minimal and maximal output conditional Rényi entropies for quantum channels.
motivation: Conditional Rényi entropies and their additivity are central to quantum information theory, with applications ranging from device-independent entanglement certification to quantum channel capacity bounds. Prior results were limited to two-indexed norms or specific parameter ranges.
method: The author defines multi-indexed Schatten spaces and establishes factorization formulas, non-commutative Minkowski inequalities, and identity-removal equalities, extending operator-space and matrix-analytic techniques to the multi-indexed quasi-normed setting.
result: The main results show that complete hypercontractivity and reverse hypercontractivity tensorize for compatible indices, and that the completely bounded minimal and maximal output conditional entropies are additive under tensor products for all compatible indices. Chain rules for smooth max-entropy are also extended to signaling channel compositions.
conclusion: This work significantly generalizes the theory of conditional Rényi entropies and their additivity, providing new mathematical tools with direct applications in quantum information, particularly for device-independent entanglement certification.

For an ordered tuple Q=(q1,...,qn) of nonzero indices, the authors define quasi-norms (for positive indices) or anti-norms (for negative indices) on operators acting on an n-fold tensor product, subject to the compatibility condition |1/qi - 1/qj| ≤ 1 for indices of the same sign. The construction extends Pisier's operator-valued Schatten norms and the recently introduced two-indexed Schatten quasi-norms. The authors establish factorization formulas that combine operator space and matrix-analytic techniques, and lift several central tools from the seminal work of Devetak, Junge, King, and Ruskai (CMP 2006) to this multi-indexed setting, including a noncommutative Minkowski inequality for swapped systems and two identity-removal equalities. As a consequence, complete hypercontractivity and complete reverse hypercontractivity are shown to tensorize for all compatible indices, including negative ones. In quantum information theory, the paper proves additivity of the completely bounded minimal and maximal output conditional entropies under tensor products of quantum channels for all α ≥ 1/2, extending previous results that held only for α > 1 or unconditionally. title: Harnessing Measurement Error As A Thermodynamic Resource In Two-Reservoir Information Engines
authors: Yang Xiao, Qian Zeng, Jin Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In general, measurement error constrains the performance of information engines. However, this may not hold universally. In this work, we propose a class of two-reservoirs information engines (TRIEs) with a two-level system and demonstrate that the monotonic relationships between the work output, the efficiency, as well as the work fluctuations of the TRIEs and measurement error are determined by the demon's control parameters. Utilizing this, we establish the conditions that allow the TRIEs to generate useful work under any level of measurement error, and identify the regimes in which these performance parameters can be optimized simultaneously by the measurement error. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when the demon's energy cost is supplied solely by the cold reservoir, the efficiency that accounts for this cost can surpass the standard Carnot bound without violating the second law. Finally, we design a dual Otto cycles TRIE and provide an experimental scheme for its implementation based on a trapped [MATH] ion. Significantly, our results can be applied to the multi-level system information engines.
tldr: The paper shows that measurement error can act as a thermodynamic resource in two-reservoir information engines, enabling useful work extraction and enhanced efficiency under certain demon control parameters.
motivation: Measurement error is usually detrimental to information engines, but the authors ask whether it can be harnessed to improve thermodynamic performance.
method: They introduce two-reservoir information engines based on a two-level system, analyze work output, efficiency, and fluctuations as functions of measurement error, and design a dual Otto cycle implementation with a trapped ion.
result: They identify conditions where useful work is generated for any measurement error, find regimes where performance parameters are simultaneously optimized by error, and show efficiency can surpass the Carnot bound when the demon's energy cost is supplied solely by the cold reservoir.
conclusion: Measurement error can be a thermodynamic resource in information engines, with potential extensions to multi-level systems and experimental realization.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a class of two-reservoir information engines (TRIEs) based on a two-level system, where a demon performs measurements with a finite error probability. The authors derive analytical expressions for the work output, efficiency, and work fluctuations as functions of the measurement error and the demon's control parameters (e.g., the energy gap and the measurement protocol). They show that the monotonicity of these performance metrics with respect to measurement error is not universal but depends on the control parameters. This allows them to identify conditions under which the engine can produce useful work even with arbitrarily large measurement error, and regimes where increasing error can simultaneously optimize work, efficiency, and fluctuations. They also consider the thermodynamic cost of the demon's measurement and show that when this cost is supplied solely by the cold reservoir, the resulting efficiency can exceed the standard Carnot bound without violating the second law. Finally, they propose a dual Otto cycle implementation using a trapped 40Ca+ ion and argue that the results extend to multi-level systems.

title: Exact Temporal Criticalities Of Entanglement And Negativity In Gaussian And Non-Gaussian Dissipative Kitaev Chains
authors: Shrey Chowdhary, Sanket Chirame, Stephan Haas, Rishabh Jha
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When the two largest eigenvalues of an entanglement or negativity spectrum meet, the gap of the corresponding entanglement or negativity Hamiltonian closes while entropies stay smooth, an event we call a temporal criticality. We ask when such criticalities occur in open fermionic systems, in which order, and whether they precede the geometric decoherence time, at which the negativity starts to fall. We compare loss and gain, which respect fermion parity only on average (weak symmetry) and keep the state Gaussian, with density dephasing, which respects it in every jump (strong symmetry) and makes the state non-Gaussian. We find that Gaussianity, rather than the symmetry, fixes the criterion for a criticality. In a Gaussian state the entanglement gap of a subsystem closes exactly when its two parity sectors carry equal weight, and the negativity gap closes exactly when this happens for the subsystem or its complement, so the negativity criticality never comes after the entanglement one. Uniform balanced loss and gain only shrink the two parities and leave both criticalities in place at every rate, for any quadratic Hamiltonian. In an open Kitaev chain, weak imbalanced loss and gain shift the criticalities by amounts set by the occupations at the cut, and at strong rates they allow a closing near the relaxation time only when an odd number of neighboring sites pass half filling. For dephasing we solve the non-Gaussian dynamics exactly at the point where the bond terms of the chain commute. Weak dephasing delays both criticalities and, away from the chain ends, moves them ahead of the parity balance, where the parity rules of Gaussian states would place them. As the dephasing rate approaches critical damping, both criticalities recede to infinite time, and at strong dephasing the negativity starts to fall long before either gap begins to shrink.
tldr: The paper identifies and characterizes exact temporal criticalities of entanglement and negativity spectra in Gaussian and non-Gaussian dissipative Kitaev chains, showing that Gaussianity fixes the criteria for when these criticalities occur.
motivation: Open fermionic systems exhibit entanglement and negativity dynamics whose spectral criticalities may precede geometric decoherence, but their occurrence and ordering were not fully understood.
method: The authors compare fermion-parity-preserving loss/gain (Gaussian dynamics) with density dephasing (non-Gaussian dynamics) in open Kitaev chains, deriving exact criteria for gap closures in the entanglement and negativity spectra, and solving the non-Gaussian dephasing dynamics exactly at a commuting point.

title: Foundational Puzzles On Quantum Universality: From Wigner's Friend To Black Holes
authors: Laurens Walleghem
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite its remarkable empirical success and predictive power, quantum theory is riddled with mysteries. One such conceptual puzzle is the measurement problem: why do quantum systems in superposition collapse to a single-valued outcome upon being measured? The scenario of Wigner's friend illustrates this tension, with recent extensions deriving strong no-go results for the nature of reality. Another fundamental puzzle arises at the interface of quantum theory and general relativity---the black hole information paradox. This thesis further explores these two foundational paradoxes. Part I of this thesis focuses on extensions of the Wigner's friend scenario. We introduce several novel extended Wigner's friend arguments, and establish connections with notions of nonclassicality, i.e. the study of quantum phenomena that evade classical explanation. Key results are a refined version of the Frauchiger--Renner paradox, new extended Wigner's friend scenarios based on contextuality, and an argument against the absoluteness of free choices based on the Pusey--Barrett--Rudolph theorem. The latter result complements the Local Friendliness no-go theorem, which challenged the absoluteness of experimentally obtained measurement outcomes. In Part II of this thesis, we turn to black hole puzzles and the interplay of quantum theory and gravity. We present a paradox that unifies extended Wigner's friend arguments with black hole puzzles, strengthening the cloning and firewall paradoxes. After discussing subtleties in these paradoxes, we next present an analysis combining elements of quantum theory with gravity, analyzing the detector response near a superposed black hole using elements of quantum reference frames.
tldr: This thesis explores foundational paradoxes from Wigner's friend to black holes, introducing extended Wigner's friend arguments and connecting them to nonclassicality and quantum gravity puzzles.
motivation: Quantum theory's measurement problem and the black hole information paradox expose deep tensions between quantum mechanics, relativity, and our notions of reality, motivating a refined analysis of no-go theorems and unified foundational arguments.
method: The thesis develops novel extended Wigner's friend scenarios based on contextuality and the Pusey-Barrett-Rudolph theorem, and analyzes detector response near a superposed black hole using quantum reference frames.
result: It yields a refined Frauchiger-Renner paradox, new contextuality-based Wigner's friend arguments, an argument against the absoluteness of free choices complementing Local Friendliness, and a paradox unifying Wigner's friend with black hole cloning and firewall paradoxes.
conclusion: The work strengthens no-go results on reality and free choice and bridges quantum foundations with quantum gravity, showing foundational puzzles remain central to quantum information theory.

title: On Information Propagation In Krylov Subspaces
authors: Pablo Martinez-Azcona, Maximilian Meyer-Moelleringhof, Adolfo Del Campo, Apollonas S. Matsoukas-Roubeas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Krylov subspace methods provide an efficient tool for modeling any quantum initial value problem as a one dimensional chain. A time ordered path formulation, in which the dynamical generator successively splits probability between paths, yields a speed limit within such dynamical subspaces. For power law growing Lanczos coefficients [MATH] we find super ballistic lightcones, with an exponentially spreading lightcone for maximal growth [MATH]. Causality in the Krylov chain constrains the Lanczos coefficients to grow at most linearly. We illustrate the validity of the above in the [MATH] and Heisenberg Weyl algebras, and in a many body skew field Ising model. Moreover, we extend the above bound to the family of [MATH] complexities. Lastly, mapping to a spin chain gives a Lieb Robinson bound analogue and opens the problem to standard condensed matter methods.
tldr: The paper develops a time-ordered path formulation of Krylov subspace dynamics, deriving a speed limit and super-ballistic lightcones for information propagation, with a Lieb-Robinson bound analogue via mapping to spin chains.
motivation: Krylov subspace methods efficiently model quantum dynamics as a one-dimensional chain, but the constraints on how information propagates within these subspaces and the resulting speed limits were not fully understood.
method: The authors introduce a time-ordered path formulation where the dynamical generator successively splits probability between paths, yielding a speed limit in Krylov space, and analyze power-law growing Lanczos coefficients to find lightcone behavior and causality constraints.
result: They find super-ballistic lightcones with exponential spreading for maximal growth, show causality restricts Lanczos coefficients to grow at most linearly, extend the bound to a family of complexities, and illustrate the results in SU(2) and Heisenberg-Weyl algebras and a many-body skew-field Ising model.
conclusion: The mapping to a spin chain provides a Lieb-Robinson bound analogue, opening Krylov subspace problems to standard condensed matter methods and establishing fundamental limits on information propagation in quantum dynamics.

For power-law growing Lanczos coefficients b_n ~ n^δ, they find super-ballistic lightcones, with an exponentially spreading lightcone for the maximal growth δ=1. They argue that causality in the Krylov chain constrains the Lanczos coefficients to grow at most linearly. The results are illustrated in the SL(2,R) and Heisenberg-Weyl algebras, and in a many-body skew field Ising model. Furthermore, they extend the bound to the family of Q complexities. Finally, they map the problem to a spin chain, obtaining a Lieb-Robinson bound analogue, which opens the problem to standard condensed matter methods.

The causality constraint is enforced by requiring that the support of the wavefunction does not exceed the causal cone defined by the path formulation. title: Quantum Machine Learning Protection Of Military Quantum Key Distribution Against Cryptographically Camouflaged Attacks
authors: Muhammad Shaheer Bin Junaid
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum key distribution proves its protocol secure and says nothing about the hardware beneath it, so military and government operators fielding it for command-and-control keys monitor the channel for implementation attacks, and that monitoring has a blind spot. An adversary with a kleptographic foothold in the generator of a public per-block value \(x=g^v \pmod p\) can hide attacked blocks in honest noise, gating them on a predicate of its discrete logarithm, making detection a discrete logarithm problem that defeats every efficient classical monitor yet yields to a quantum kernel recovering \(v\) through Shor's algorithm. I formalise these cryptographically camouflaged attacks, reduce their hardness to an established learning separation, prove a single-frequency fidelity kernel cannot represent an interval predicate, and test them on Ghillie, a decoy-state BB84 simulator with a positive key rate to 142 km. From 10- to 14-bit groups over two seeds, a classical monitor reads 0.458 to 0.516 on camouflaged attacks while the quantum kernel reads 1.000, and both catch overt attacks above 0.99. Finite-precision recovery under depolarising noise and a hardened predicate lower the quantum result to 0.916 through 0.983 with the classical monitor at chance, and a feasibility probe on IBM Heron processors tracks the exact kernel within 0.034. A defender can therefore discard precisely the compromised key material, although the advantage is asymptotic, awaits fault tolerance, and holds only when the feature map matches the adversary's predicate, since a low-frequency map reads 0.545 on a residue pattern and 0.982 once aligned.
tldr: The paper formalizes cryptographically camouflaged attacks on QKD and shows that a quantum kernel can detect them where classical monitors fail.
motivation: QKD security proofs ignore hardware-level implementation attacks, and current channel monitoring has a blind spot for adversaries with a kleptographic foothold in public value generation.
method: The authors reduce the attack detection problem to a learning separation, prove a single-frequency fidelity kernel cannot represent an interval predicate, and test on a decoy-state BB84 simulator with classical and quantum kernel monitors.
result: Classical monitors perform at chance on camouflaged attacks while the quantum kernel achieves perfect detection (0.916–0.983 under finite-precision noise and hardened predicates), with IBM Heron processors tracking the ideal kernel within 0.034.
conclusion: A defender can selectively discard compromised key material, but the advantage is asymptotic, requires fault tolerance, and depends on matching the feature map to the adversary's predicate.

This makes detection a discrete logarithm problem that is hard for classical monitors but solvable by a quantum kernel using Shor's algorithm. The author reduces the hardness of these attacks to an established learning separation, proves that a single-frequency fidelity kernel cannot represent an interval predicate, and tests the attacks on Ghillie, a decoy-state BB84 simulator with a positive key rate up to 142 km. Results show that a classical monitor performs near chance (0.458–0.516) on camouflaged attacks, while the quantum kernel achieves perfect detection (1.000). Under finite-precision recovery, depolarising noise, and a hardened predicate, the quantum kernel's performance drops to 0.916–0.983, still far above classical chance. A feasibility probe on IBM Heron processors tracks the exact kernel within 0.034. The paper concludes that a defender can discard compromised key material, but the advantage is asymptotic, requires fault tolerance, and depends on the feature map matching the adversary's predicate.

title: Magic Quantum Code Surgery
authors: Kathleen Chang, Anasuya Lyons, Yuanjie Ren, Harald Putterman, Nathanan Tantivasadakarn, Victor V. Albert, Benjamin J. Brown, Dominic J. Williamson
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Clifford operations required for universal quantum computation can be implemented by measuring logical Clifford operators. We present a generalized framework to fault-tolerantly measure transversal Clifford logical operators in quantum low-density parity check (QLDPC) codes. Our protocol takes any QLDPC code and deforms the code across additional ancillary qubits such that a product of stabilizers measures the desired logical Clifford operator. We prove that the deformed, Clifford-stabilized code remains LDPC and that its distance is preserved up to a constant factor independent of the number of physical qubits. We further prove that the Clifford measurement has a fault distance against data qubit and measurement errors that grows linearly with the distance of the original code. We apply our methods to implement logical non-Clifford gates in algorithmically relevant subroutines and to prepare magic states in quantum stabilizer codes.
tldr: A generalized framework for fault-tolerantly measuring transversal Clifford logical operators in QLDPC codes to implement non-Clifford gates and prepare magic states.
motivation: Universal quantum computation requires non-Clifford operations, which can be implemented by measuring logical Clifford operators, but doing so fault-tolerantly in QLDPC codes remains challenging.
method: The protocol deforms any QLDPC code across ancillary qubits so that a product of stabilizers measures a desired logical Clifford operator, with proofs that the deformed code stays LDPC and preserves distance up to a constant factor.

title: Optimal Phase Control Of A Measurement-assisted Quantum Refrigerator
authors: Jinkai Liu, Xian He, Jizhou He, Jianhui Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04237v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A tilted nonselective measurement can close the upper transition of a three-level quantum refrigerator, but it also generates coherence that feeds back on the populations and suppresses the cooling current. We formulate randomized open-loop control of the measurement azimuthal phase \(\alpha\), sampled independently at each event from a probability distribution \(P(\alpha)\), while keeping the event rate, polar angle, and single-event population-transfer probability fixed. Direct population transfer is phase independent, whereas the coherence source carries the factor \(e^{-i\alpha}\). Exact elimination of the stationary coherence gives \(0\leq k_{\rm eff}[P]\leq A_m\), where \(k_{\rm eff}[P]\) is the effective population-transfer rate between the upper levels and \(A_m\) is the bare direct mixing rate. When the fixed measurement couples populations and coherence, the upper bound is attained if and only if \(\langle e^{i\alpha}\rangle_P=0\), where \(\langle\cdot\rangle_P\) denotes an average over the phase distribution. The minimal realization uses two equally weighted phases separated by \(\pi\): the population-to-coherence source and its return to the populations then vanish at the generator level, while the full direct mixing remains. Because the cold current increases strictly with \(k_{\rm eff}\) in the refrigeration window, the same condition maximizes the stationary cooling power over the independent random-phase distributions considered here. For one representative parameter set, phase cycling increases the fixed-gap cooling power by about \(32\%\) relative to a fixed-phase measurement, while leaving the ratio of extracted cold heat to supplied measurement energy unchanged.
tldr: Randomized control of the measurement azimuthal phase optimizes a measurement-assisted three-level quantum refrigerator by eliminating coherence feedback and maximizing the stationary cooling power.
motivation: A tilted nonselective measurement can close the upper transition of a three-level quantum refrigerator, but the coherence it generates feeds back on populations and suppresses the cooling current, motivating a control strategy for the measurement phase.
method: The azimuthal phase α is treated as independently sampled from a probability distribution P(α) while fixing event rate, polar angle, and population-transfer probability; exact elimination of stationary coherence yields an effective population-transfer rate k_eff[P] and a condition for its maximum.

conclusion: Phase cycling provides an optimal open-loop control for the measurement-assisted quantum refrigerator, achieving maximal stationary cooling power under independent random-phase distributions.

title: Indistinguishability Lifting For Keyed Oracles, Compressed Ideal Cipher, And More Applications
authors: Yu-Hsuan Huang Ritam Bhaumik
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryptographic security proofs often involve an adversary interacting with a larger, keyed oracle that consists of (potentially exponentially) many independent instances of a smaller, base oracle. However, showing quantum indistinguishability between two such keyed oracles can be tricky, since a single query made by an adversary may involve a superposition that covers all instances of the base oracles simultaneously. In this paper, we establish a generic indistinguishability lifting theorem of the following form: if the two base oracles are indistinguishable under quantum queries, then their corresponding keyed oracles are too, up to an O(q^2) multiplicative loss in distinguishing advantage, where q is the number of queries made by the adversary. Our lifting theorem applies to both statistical and computational settings, and to oracles that are stateful as well. It is also optimal in that it matches the obvious Grover search attack for a certain (contrived) choice of oracles. As an immediate application, we extend Carolan's compressed permutation oracle to an efficiently implementable compressed ideal cipher, and use it to prove preimage resistance of the Davies-Meyer compression function in the quantum ideal cipher model. Thanks to our lifting theorem, the soundness of our compressed ideal cipher reduces to that of Carolan's oracle, and any further improvement on the latter would automatically carry over to the former. As our second application, we give a modular construction that doubles the message length of any quantum-secure strong pseudorandom permutation. Along the way, we show that an existing two-round tweakable Feistel construction is indistinguishable from a random permutation under quantum bidirectional queries. This is done via a dedicated polynomial-method argument, which may be of independent interest.
tldr: The paper establishes a generic indistinguishability lifting theorem for keyed oracles under quantum queries, enabling applications to compressed ideal ciphers and quantum-secure pseudorandom permutations.
motivation: Quantum adversaries can query superpositions across all instances of a keyed oracle, making it difficult to prove indistinguishability between keyed oracles even when their base oracles are indistinguishable.
method: The authors prove a lifting theorem showing that if base oracles are quantum-indistinguishable, then keyed oracles are too, with an O(q^2) loss in distinguishing advantage, covering statistical, computational, and stateful settings, and use a polynomial-method argument for tweakable Feistel.

conclusion: The lifting theorem reduces the soundness of the compressed ideal cipher to that of Carolan's oracle, so future improvements carry over, and the polynomial-method argument may be of independent interest.

title: Modular Neural Decoder For Surface Code Memory And Logic On Superconducting Processors
authors: Moritz Lange, Ole Fjelds{\aa}, Gustaf Jonasson Johansson, Mats Granath
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural decoders for quantum error correction have achieved high accuracy on surface code memory experiments, but practical fault-tolerant computation requires decoders that transfer across devices, noise conditions, and logical operations. We introduce a modular graph-recurrent decoder designed for this setting. Built from reusable local syndrome encoders, it is pretrained in simulation and fine-tuned to hardware using a common pipeline, with only lightweight spatial aggregation adapted between experiments. The decoder performs competitively on conventional memory benchmarks, outperforming minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) at distances 3 and 5 on an IBM Nighthawk-generation processor and closely approaching AlphaQubit on Google's below-threshold hardware data. We then test the framework in two settings beyond memory decoding on the same IBM device. First, in an [MATH]-type stability experiment, we continuously tune the effective measurement error rate using a variable pre-readout rotation and train a single decoder jointly across the resulting noise range. It matches or outperforms MWPM across the sweep without requiring a separately calibrated decoder for each setting. Second, we decode a [MATH]-merge lattice-surgery experiment between two distance-3 surface-code patches, improving the decoded correlation between the merge outcome and the final [MATH] parity relative to MWPM on real hardware. Together, these experiments demonstrate neural decoding that is portable not only across hardware, but also across qualitatively different surface code observables and logical operations, using models trainable on single-GPU academic resources.
tldr: A modular graph-recurrent neural decoder for surface code quantum error correction transfers across superconducting hardware, noise conditions, and logical operations, outperforming MWPM in memory, stability, and lattice-surgery experiments.
motivation: Practical fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that can be reused across devices, noise regimes, and logical operations rather than being recalibrated for each setting.
method: The authors build a modular graph-recurrent decoder from reusable local syndrome encoders, pretrain it in simulation, fine-tune it on hardware with lightweight spatial aggregation, and evaluate it on IBM and Google superconducting processors.
result: The decoder matches or outperforms minimum-weight perfect matching on distance-3 and distance-5 memory benchmarks, approaches AlphaQubit on Google data, and improves decoding in an M-type stability experiment and a lattice-surgery merge experiment.
conclusion: Neural decoding can be portable across hardware and qualitatively different surface-code observables and logical operations while remaining trainable on single-GPU academic resources.

title: Generalised Bit-Vector Abstractions For Formal Verification Of Quantum Error-Detection And Entanglement Circuits Over {h,x,c-not}: Css Constructions, Soundness, And Mutation-Based Validation
authors: Arun Govindankutty
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Formal verification of quantum circuits becomes difficult as circuit size grows because exhaustive reasoning over the Hilbert space is computationally expensive. In previous work [1], we introduced a bit-vector abstraction that separates superposition tracking from basis-state behavior, enabling SMT-based verification of fixed-size error-detection and entanglement circuits built from H, X, and C-NOT gates. This paper extends the framework in five directions. First, we generalise correctness properties to parametrised repetition and concatenated phase-flip codes with up to 101 logical elements. Second, we verify syndrome extraction for CSS codes specified by arbitrary parity-check matrices, including the Steane, [[15,7,3]] Hamming, [[15,1,3]] Reed-Muller, and rotated surface codes with distances up to 101. We consider arbitrary error patterns, detection up to a specified weight, and recovery using a classical decoder, with counterexamples beyond each code's correction or detection capability. Third, we characterize the {H,X,C-NOT} fragment for which the abstraction faithfully represents Hilbert-space semantics. We prove soundness, demonstrate necessity with counterexamples, validate the characterisation against state-vector simulation, and prove the six lemmas from the original work. Fourth, a mutation study using 13 operators identifies equivalent mutants and detects all 622 non-equivalent mutants within the evaluated fault model. Fifth, a direct Z3 implementation verifies GHZ circuits with up to 262,144 qubits across three topologies on a 16GB laptop. Random H+C-NOT networks show verification cost rises sharply with depth when outputs depend on many inputs. The approach does not target general stabilizer circuits, Y-type stabilizers, fault-tolerant protocols, or physical noise; we identify extensions needed to address these cases.
tldr: This paper extends a bit-vector abstraction for SMT-based formal verification of quantum error-detection and entanglement circuits built from H, X, and C-NOT gates to parametrised codes and CSS syndrome extraction.

title: Information Entropy And Dissipation Potential In Stochastic Nambu Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics
authors: Tatsuaki Wada So Katagiri
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the relationship between the dissipation potential [MATH] and information entropy in stochastic Nambu nonequilibrium thermodynamics (NNET). Starting from pure diffusion, gradient-flow systems, and systems with Hamiltonian rotational currents, we derive the stationary distribution of the Fokker--Planck equation including a Nambu flow. We show that, when the Nambu flow preserves the dissipation potential and an Einstein-type relation holds between the diffusion matrix and the transport tensor, the stationary distribution is governed by an exponential weight determined by [MATH]. Consequently, the local self-information is directly related to the dissipation potential, demonstrating that [MATH] should not be identified with the Shannon entropy itself but instead serves as the stationary quasipotential governing the nonequilibrium steady-state distribution. Using the distinction between the thermodynamic entropy and the dissipation potential established for an open gas--piston system coupled to a thermal bath and an external-pressure reservoir, we further clarify the Massieu interpretation of [MATH], introduce a Nambu canonical distribution, and derive the covariance of fluctuations within the saddle-point approximation. These results provide a statistical interpretation of the NNET dissipation potential by identifying it as the stationary quasipotential underlying nonequilibrium steady states.
tldr: The paper establishes a statistical link between the dissipation potential and local self-information in stochastic Nambu nonequilibrium thermodynamics, identifying the former as the stationary quasipotential of the nonequilibrium steady state.
motivation: To clarify how information entropy relates to the dissipation potential in nonequilibrium thermodynamics, which is often conflated with Shannon entropy.
method: Derives the stationary distribution of the Fokker-Planck equation with a Nambu flow under a dissipation-potential-preserving condition and an Einstein relation, and uses an open gas-piston model and saddle-point approximation.
result: Shows that local self-information is directly tied to the dissipation potential, which governs the stationary distribution via an exponential weight, and derives a Nambu canonical distribution and fluctuation covariance.
conclusion: The dissipation potential should be interpreted not as Shannon entropy but as a stationary quasipotential underlying nonequilibrium steady states, providing a statistical interpretation of NNET.

title: How To Distinguish Chaos From Integrability Using Otoc
authors: Anders Wallberg Alexey Milekhin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The decay of out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) to a small residual value signals the scrambling of quantum information. This behavior is generic: it occurs in both chaotic and interacting integrable many-body systems, and therefore cannot by itself distinguish between them. In this paper we analytically study the late-time saturation value of a closely related observable, operator purity, and show that its scaling with system size robustly distinguishes chaotic from integrable systems. Our approach is based on the Mazur bound, which provides concrete scaling estimates and makes explicit why the locality of integrable charges matters. We support our findings with numerical simulations of one-dimensional spin chains.
tldr: The paper shows that the late-time saturation scaling of operator purity, unlike OTOC decay, distinguishes chaotic from integrable many-body systems.
motivation: OTOC decay to a small residual value is generic in both chaotic and integrable systems, so another observable is needed to robustly distinguish them.
method: The authors analytically study the late-time operator purity using the Mazur bound and support the findings with numerical simulations of one-dimensional spin chains.
result: Operator purity scaling with system size separates chaotic and integrable cases, with the locality of integrable charges playing a central role.
conclusion: Operator purity provides a reliable diagnostic for chaos versus integrability, with implications for quantum information scrambling and thermalization.

The authors propose that the late-time saturation value of a closely related observable, operator purity, exhibits a scaling with system size that robustly distinguishes chaotic from integrable systems. They analytically study this saturation value using the Mazur bound, which provides concrete scaling estimates and highlights the role of locality of integrable charges. The analysis is supported by numerical simulations of one-dimensional spin chains, demonstrating that operator purity saturates to a value that decays polynomially with system size in integrable systems, while in chaotic systems it saturates to a value that is exponentially small in system size. This work provides a new diagnostic for quantum chaos and sheds light on the role of local conserved quantities in scrambling.

The Mazur bound is particularly suited because it explicitly incorporates the locality of conserved charges, allowing the authors to show that local charges lead to a polynomial scaling of the saturation value with system size, whereas non-local or absent charges (as in chaotic systems) lead to exponential suppression. title: Gate-Based Quantum Simulation Of Finite-Temperature Open-System Dynamics: A Post-Processing Reconstruction Approach For Collision Models
authors: Chikako Uchiyama Kazunari Hashimoto
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating open-system dynamics on gate-based quantum computers offers a route to exploring dissipative quantum phenomena through programmable quantum processing. Collision models provide a direct and flexible framework by representing the environment through sequential system--ancilla collisions. At finite temperatures, however, they typically require repeated preparation of thermal ancillas, adding circuit overhead and gate errors. Here, we show that, for a broad class of [MATH]-symmetric system--ancilla interactions, finite-temperature dynamics can instead be reconstructed from simulations with pure ancillas in orthogonal basis states. The target temperature enters only through classical post-processing of the resulting pure-branch data, allowing the same data to be reused for different temperatures without additional quantum processing. Bypassing explicit thermal-state preparation reduces ancilla-preparation overhead and preparation-induced errors.
tldr: A gate-based quantum simulation method reconstructs finite-temperature open-system dynamics in collision models from pure-ancilla data via classical post-processing, avoiding thermal-state preparation.
motivation: Simulating finite-temperature open-system dynamics on gate-based quantum computers is hindered by the need to repeatedly prepare thermal ancillas, which adds circuit overhead and gate errors.
method: For a broad class of U(1)-symmetric system-ancilla interactions, the authors simulate pure ancillas prepared in orthogonal basis states and reconstruct the finite-temperature dynamics through classical post-processing of the resulting pure-branch data.
result: The same pure-branch data can be reused to obtain dynamics at different temperatures without additional quantum processing, reducing ancilla-preparation overhead and preparation-induced errors.
conclusion: This post-processing reconstruction approach enables more efficient finite-temperature open-system simulation on gate-based quantum processors by bypassing explicit thermal-state preparation.

title: Predicting Noise In A Trapped-ion Quantum Simulation Of A Lattice Gauge Theory
authors: Hassan Ugail
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A recent trapped-ion experiment realised a lattice gauge theory in which the internal states of the ions carry the gauge field and their vibrations carry bosonic matter. In that experiment, a charge moving around a loop was frozen in place by Aharonov--Bohm interference. The noise of such a device is usually simulated after the measurements have been made. Here we show that it can be predicted before the machine is run. For each quantity that the experiment measures, we derive, from the reported noise rates alone, a formula for how it decays together with a bound it can never exceed. The results reveal a simple pattern. The local conservation law of the theory is a parity of the vibrational mode, so heating violates it at a rate that grows as the mode warms, and the violation accelerates rather than accumulating steadily. At zero electric field, each of the three noise processes of the device leaves its own fingerprint. Heating affects only the conservation law, motional dephasing only the interference, and qubit errors only the stored flux and the frozen state. Once the electric field is switched on, the frozen state begins to leak, and we write an exact formula and a guaranteed bound for that leak.
tldr: The paper derives analytic formulas and bounds to predict how noise affects measurable quantities in a trapped-ion quantum simulation of a lattice gauge theory, revealing distinct fingerprints of heating, dephasing, and qubit errors.
motivation: Trapped-ion quantum simulators of lattice gauge theories are subject to noise that is typically simulated only after measurements; predicting it beforehand can help interpret results and identify error sources.
method: Using reported noise rates, the authors analytically derive decay formulas and guaranteed bounds for each measured quantity, analyzing parity conservation, heating, motional dephasing, qubit errors, and electric-field-induced leakage.
result: They find that heating violates the vibrational parity conservation law at an accelerating rate, each noise process has a unique signature at zero electric field, and switching on the electric field causes leakage in the frozen state with an exact formula and bound.
conclusion: The work enables a priori noise prediction for trapped-ion lattice gauge theory simulations and provides a framework for understanding noise fingerprints and conservation-law violations in such experiments.

title: Driven-Dissipative Ground State Preparation: Mixing Time And Randomness
authors: Paul Cazeaux, Marius Junge, Diyi Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dissipative protocols offer a route to ground state preparation that does not require a large initial overlap with the ground state. To move beyond time independent Lindbladians and randomized Lindbladians sampled from a fixed distribution, we study driven-dissipative protocols in which the generator varies over time. Our construction uses a family of randomized Lindbladians whose jump operators are obtained by averaging the unitary evolution of random matrices under a fixed target Hamiltonian. We show that empirical averages of these Lindbladians drive arbitrary initial density matrices to low energy states. The resulting mixing time bounds depend on the Hamiltonian only through its eigenvalue distribution and remain valid even for cold starts.
tldr: The paper introduces driven-dissipative protocols using randomized time-varying Lindbladians to prepare low-energy states with mixing-time bounds independent of initial overlap.
motivation: Dissipative ground state preparation typically requires time-independent or fixed-distribution Lindbladians; the authors aim to extend this to time-varying generators and cold starts.
method: They construct randomized Lindbladians from averaging unitary evolutions of random matrices under a target Hamiltonian, and analyze the mixing time of the resulting empirical average channel.
result: Empirical averages drive arbitrary initial density matrices to low-energy states, with mixing times depending only on the Hamiltonian's eigenvalue distribution and remaining valid for cold starts.
conclusion: This provides a flexible dissipative state-preparation framework with rigorous convergence guarantees beyond static Lindbladians.

The empirical average of these Lindbladians over many samples is shown to drive arbitrary initial density matrices to low-energy states of H. title: Interaction-Aware Embedding Optimization For Neutral-Atom Quantum Processors
authors: Cl\'ement de Terrasson de Montleau, Victor Drouin-Touchette, Wesley Coelho
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neutral atom-based quantum computers have the ability to dynamically reshape the qubit register geometry between experimental runs. This capability enables different types of problems to be mapped directly onto the hardware, significantly enhancing the efficiency of solving, for instance, complex optimization and machine learning use-cases. However, this flexibility requires finding atom positions to implement target pairwise interactions, inducing a difficult nonconvex optimization for setting up the quantum machine. In this work, we introduce a new force-directed method that targets interactions to encode the input problem on the quantum computer. Numerical results show that our new method can improve embedding feasibility and solution quality by orders of magnitude, and remains reliable on the largest instances.
tldr: Introduces a force-directed embedding optimization method to position atoms in neutral-atom quantum processors for encoding target pairwise interactions.
motivation: Neutral-atom quantum computers can dynamically reshape qubit register geometry, but finding atom positions that realize desired pairwise interactions is a difficult nonconvex optimization problem.
method: Develops an interaction-aware force-directed algorithm that optimizes atom positions to match target interaction graphs on the quantum processor.
result: Numerical results show order-of-magnitude improvements in embedding feasibility and solution quality, remaining reliable on the largest tested instances.
conclusion: The method enables more efficient mapping of optimization and machine learning problems onto neutral-atom quantum hardware.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the problem of embedding a target interaction graph onto a neutral-atom quantum computer by positioning atoms in a 2D plane such that the resulting pairwise interactions (e.g., Rydberg blockade or dipole-dipole) match the desired couplings. The authors propose a new force-directed method that treats atom positions as particles subject to attractive and repulsive forces derived from the difference between target and actual interaction strengths. The method iteratively updates positions to minimize a cost function that penalizes deviations from the target pairwise interactions, while respecting physical constraints such as minimum atom separation and maximum interaction range. The paper reports numerical experiments on a variety of graph instances, including random graphs and structured problems, and compares the new method against existing approaches such as simulated annealing and gradient-based optimization. The results show that the force-directed method improves embedding feasibility (the fraction of instances successfully embedded) and solution quality (e.g., fidelity of the encoded interactions) by orders of magnitude, and remains reliable on the largest instances tested (up to hundreds of atoms). The authors claim that this enables more efficient mapping of optimization and machine learning problems onto neutral-atom hardware, where dynamic register geometry is a key advantage.

title: Parallelizing Dissipative Quantum Algorithms
authors: Sudatta Hor, Nathan Wiebe, Yongshan Ding
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inspired by classical Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, dissipative quantum algorithms are an emerging class of methods for preparing quantum states on a quantum computer. They operate by simulating a dissipative process governed by a mathematical operator known as the Lindbladian. The performance of these algorithms can be limited by the sequential implementation of the Lindbladian's constituent jump operators, which leads to high circuit depth. To address this issue, this work analyzes a parallelization scheme to implement jump operators simultaneously. We leverage the structure of geometric locality to show that individual jump operators remain spatially localized. This exponentially reduces the circuit depth per time step, resulting in an overall polynomial improvement. Numerical experiments demonstrate a 53x reduction in query depth for a 1D benchmark system of 100 qubits. The reduced circuit depth makes dissipative algorithms more practical for near-term quantum computing.
tldr: The paper proposes a parallelization scheme for dissipative quantum algorithms that exploits the geometric locality of Lindbladian jump operators to drastically reduce circuit depth.
motivation: Dissipative quantum algorithms for state preparation are limited by the sequential implementation of jump operators, which leads to high circuit depth and hinders near-term practicality.
method: The authors analyze a parallelization scheme where jump operators are implemented simultaneously, using the spatial locality of the Lindbladian to keep each operator localized, and validate it with numerical experiments on a 1D benchmark system.
result: For a 100-qubit 1D system, the scheme achieves a 53x reduction in query depth, corresponding to an overall polynomial improvement in circuit depth.
conclusion: The reduced circuit depth makes dissipative quantum algorithms more practical for near-term quantum computing, though the focus is on algorithmic parallelization rather than thermodynamic aspects.

title: Realizing Braided Fusion 2-Categories As (3+1)d Mixed-State Topological Orders
authors: Ryohei Kobayashi, Abhinav Prem, Matthew Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct large families of mixed-state topological orders in (3+1)D, including intrinsically mixed-state topological orders. We realize these theories by relating the data parameterizing braided fusion 2-categories to the strong higher-form symmetries and their anomalies that characterize mixed-state topological order. We focus here on bosonic theories, which include theories which admit an emergent fermion in the spectrum of line operators. Our general framework is exemplified on the lattice, where we present concrete models and identify how the data of braided fusion 2-categories are physically encoded. We then formalize this data and show that every braided fusion 2-category arises from a general construction (decoherence followed by strong and weak gauging) as the category of topological operators of a (3+1)D mixed state, with intrinsically mixed-state topological orders distinguished by the presence of strong higher-form symmetries whose anomalies cannot be realized in any (3+1)D gapped ground state. Notably, we show that (3+1)D admits a new mechanism with no (2+1)D counterpart: intrinsically mixed-state order whose topological operators braid non-degenerately, but which carries a gravitational anomaly.
tldr: The paper constructs large families of (3+1)D mixed-state topological orders by mapping braided fusion 2-category data to strong higher-form symmetries and anomalies.
motivation: There is growing interest in topological order beyond pure ground states, especially intrinsically mixed-state topological orders that cannot arise in gapped quantum ground states, but a systematic classification in higher dimensions was missing.
method: The authors relate the algebraic data of braided fusion 2-categories to strong higher-form symmetries and their anomalies, provide explicit lattice models, and formalize a general construction via decoherence followed by strong and weak gauging.
result: Every braided fusion 2-category is realized as the category of topological operators of a (3+1)D mixed state; intrinsically mixed-state orders are distinguished by anomalous strong higher-form symmetries, and a new (3+1)D mechanism is found with non-degenerate braiding and a gravitational anomaly.
conclusion: The work establishes a categorical framework for mixed-state topological order in 3+1 dimensions, revealing novel phenomena without (2+1)D analogues and connecting higher category theory to symmetry and anomaly classification.

title: Q-merge: Parallelising Quantum State Preparation For Large-Scale Classical Data

title: Energy-filtered Readout Preserves Gap-enhanced Sensing In Interacting Quantum Dots
authors: Shirwan Abdullah
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A small excitation gap makes a quantum dot a sensitive probe of a weak electric field, but the charge detector that reads the probe can also excite it. We ask how much of this gap enhancement survives continuous readout, for two interacting electrons tuned through a confinement-driven crossover in a gate-defined quantum dot, using a weak-coupling, stationary two-level model. The answer depends on the energy structure of the detector, not only on its noise. A quantum point contact measures more strongly at higher bias, but once the bias energy exceeds the gap it also excites the probe. When this back-action dominates the probe's own relaxation, the optimised mean-current information rate grows only as the inverse of the gap. A sensor quantum dot with a narrow level instead reaches full measurement strength at a bias below the gap, where, for a non-interacting detector and to second order in the coupling, it cannot excite the probe at zero temperature. This energy-filtered readout keeps the inverse-square gap dependence of the quantum Fisher information, down to a gap set by the detector's level width and the electron temperature. Through such a detector the interacting pair gives about three times the information rate of a single electron with the same gap and detector, compared with 1.6-1.7 in the quantum Fisher information, for both contact and Coulomb-type interactions. These different gap dependences, and the different optimal biases of the two detectors, can be tested by bias and gate sweeps on suitably tuned charge-sensed double dots.
tldr: Energy-filtered readout by a sensor quantum dot preserves the inverse-square gap enhancement of quantum Fisher information in charge sensing of interacting electrons, whereas a quantum point contact degrades it to inverse-gap scaling once bias exceeds the gap.
motivation: A small excitation gap makes a quantum dot a sensitive probe of weak electric fields, but the charge detector used for readout can also excite the probe and spoil the enhancement.
method: A weak-coupling stationary two-level model for two interacting electrons in a gate-defined quantum dot, comparing a quantum point contact and a sensor quantum dot as detectors, computing mean-current information rate and quantum Fisher information.
result: The quantum point contact excites the probe when bias exceeds the gap, leaving only inverse-gap scaling; the sensor quantum dot with a narrow level reaches full measurement strength below the gap, preserving inverse-square gap dependence down to a gap set by detector level width and electron temperature, with the interacting pair giving about three times the information rate of a single electron.
conclusion: The detector's energy structure, not only its noise, determines how much gap enhancement survives continuous readout, and the predicted differences in gap dependence and optimal bias are testable by bias and gate sweeps on charge-sensed double dots.

title: Accelerated Search For Global Extrema In Structured Quantum Signals
authors: Katepalli R. Sreenivasan Sachin S. Bharadwaj
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extreme values of a physical system are rare by definition, yet they can govern some of its most consequential and anomalous behavior. Their sparsity makes them particularly costly to identify in large data sets. Quantum computation offers a potential way to reduce this cost. The challenge is that quantum amplitudes cannot simply be read, copied, compared, or marked using conventional search oracles. Here we introduce an algorithm for searching amplitude-encoded quantum signals that exploits their underlying structure. Through a nonlinear amplitude transformation, the algorithm identifies and certifies a global extremum while exponentially reducing the effective search space for structured signals. We establish a polylogarithmic query complexity in the data size [MATH], together with global completeness, efficient classical verification, and a measurable criterion for quantifying exploitable structure. We demonstrate the framework using computational turbulence data. Applied to line cuts of velocity gradients from a [MATH] simulation containing more than one billion grid points, the algorithm consistently isolates the extreme tail and reduces the median search space to [MATH]. The clustered structure characteristic of turbulence further accelerates the search. These results establish a direct connection between physical structure and quantum advantage in extreme-value search. For accessibility, the main text emphasizes the central ideas and results, while the theoretical derivations are provided in the Appendices.
tldr: Introduces a quantum algorithm for finding global extrema in structured amplitude-encoded signals with polylogarithmic query complexity and demonstrates it on turbulence data.
motivation: Extreme values are rare but consequential, and identifying them in large datasets is costly. Quantum search could reduce this cost, but standard oracles fail because quantum amplitudes cannot be directly read, copied, compared, or marked.
method: The algorithm exploits underlying structure via a nonlinear amplitude transformation to identify and certify a global extremum, with global completeness, efficient classical verification, and a criterion for quantifying exploitable structure.
result: It achieves polylogarithmic query complexity in the data size, exponentially reduces the effective search space for structured signals, and isolates the extreme tail in a turbulence simulation with over one billion grid points.
conclusion: The work establishes a direct connection between physical structure and quantum advantage in extreme-value search, with potential applications to structured quantum signals.

title: Frequency-Axis Calibration Via Autler-Townes Splitting In An Electromagnetically Induced Transparency Feature
authors: Stone B. Oliver, Noah Schlossberger, Tate Mcdonald, Christopher L. Holloway, Nikunjkumar Prajapati
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg atom-based electrometry is a pivotal technology that enables radio-frequency (rf) field measurements traceable to the International System of Units. This is typically accomplished by converting the direct rf power measurement of classical probes to a frequency measurement referenced to two well-defined spectral features, a commercial wavemeter, or narrow cavity lines produced via clock disciplined electro-optic modulators, although there exist cases where none of these are available. In this article, we demonstrate that a known rf frequency scale can be used to infer a laser's frequency scan using Autler-Townes (AT) splitting. In other words, we show that frequency-axis calibration can be achieved using the avoided-crossing behavior of near-resonant rf radiation. The relative separation between AT-split features is measured as a function of an applied rf field's power and detuning from atomic resonance. These peak separations are then fit to a simple, two-level model using a weighted nonlinear least-squares regression analysis that utilizes three fitting parameters, one of which is the desired calibration factor. While we do not benchmark this method against an absolute frequency reference, we do show that this method is (1) consistent with calibration via known fine-structure separation to within approximately 1.11% or better, and (2) robust against substantial experimental deviation from the system's known rf power dependence.
tldr: Demonstrates frequency-axis calibration of a laser scan using Autler-Townes splitting in a Rydberg-atom EIT feature, achieving ~1.11% agreement with fine-structure calibration.
motivation: Rydberg atom-based electrometry requires reliable frequency calibration when standard references such as wavemeters or cavity lines are unavailable.
method: Measures Autler-Townes peak separations as functions of applied RF power and frequency.

title: Nonuniform Qcph Collapse Implies Qcph Collapse
authors: Jeremy Ahrens Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite the importance of the non-uniform Polynomial-Time Hierarchy (PH/poly) in classical complexity understanding the collapse conditions of the Polynomial-Time Hierarchy (PH), a quantum equivalent of PH/poly has yet to be studied in the literature. We introduce the non-uniform computational Quantum Polynomial-Time Hierarchy (QCPH/mpoly), the quantum equivalent of PH/poly, and show that it collapses if and only if QCPH, the quantum equivalent of PH introduced by Gharibian et al. (comput. complex. 2022), also collapses. We also show that QCPH collapses if coQCMA is contained in QCMA/mpoly. These results are analogous to those of Yap (TCS 1983) commonly used to invoke the collapse of PH in classical complexity. QCPH/mpoly is analogous to QCPH with non-uniform quantum verifier circuits.
tldr: The paper introduces a non-uniform quantum polynomial-time hierarchy QCPH/mpoly and proves its collapse is equivalent to the collapse of QCPH.
motivation: Classical complexity theory uses PH/poly to study non-uniform collapse conditions of PH, but no quantum analogue has been studied until now.
method: The authors define QCPH/mpoly with non-uniform quantum verifier circuits, analogous to classical PH/poly, and prove equivalence between QCPH/mpoly and QCPH collapse, plus a sufficient condition involving coQCMA and QCMA/mpoly.
result: They show that QCPH/mpoly collapses if and only if QCPH collapses, and that QCPH collapses if coQCMA is contained in QCMA/mpoly.
conclusion: These results mirror Yap's classical theorems for PH collapse and extend quantum complexity theory, but the topic is not central to the researcher's quantum information interests.

title: Reduced Cost Quantum Kernel Training
authors: Daniel R. Germain, Benjamin Goldweber, Kayla J. Rodriguez, Kristen Rhinehardt
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum kernel methods are promising for near-term quantum machine learning, but their training costs are driven by the quadratic scaling of Gram-matrix construction and the measurement cost of estimating individual kernel values. In this work, we investigate one-class anomaly detection as a resource-efficient operating regime for training non-variational quantum kernel models. Using the ULB Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset, we evaluate three quantum feature maps across training-set sizes and qubit counts. Power-law saturation models reveal strong diminishing returns with increasing training data, with 500-sample models retaining approximately 90--93\% of their fitted asymptotic average precision (AP). We further observe no severe exponential concentration among the evaluated feature maps over the investigated qubit range, thereby avoiding the exponentially increasing measurement requirements associated with that regime. Finally, Nystr\"om approximation reduces kernel construction from [MATH] to [MATH] evaluations, with QSVR retaining 94--97\% of its exact-kernel AP using only five landmarks. For ZZ-QSVR, downsampling from 4,000 to 500 training samples and applying a five-landmark approximation decreases the number of required kernel evaluations from approximately [MATH] million to [MATH], a reduction of more than 3,200-fold, while AP decreases from [MATH] to [MATH]. Under the minimum IonQ pricing assumption considered here, this corresponds to an illustrative reduction in quantum kernel training cost from approximately \[MATH]417{,}480. These results demonstrate that training-set reduction and low-rank approximation can substantially reduce the resources required to train non-variational quantum kernel anomaly detectors while retaining meaningful anomaly-discrimination performance.
tldr: The paper evaluates cost-reduction strategies for training non-variational quantum kernel anomaly detectors, showing that training-set reduction and Nyström approximation can cut kernel evaluations by thousands of times with modest performance loss.
motivation: Quantum kernel methods are promising for near-term quantum machine learning, but their training costs are dominated by quadratic Gram-matrix construction and repeated kernel-value estimation.
method: Using the ULB Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset, the authors evaluate three quantum feature maps across training-set sizes and qubit counts, fit power-law saturation models, and apply Nyström low-rank approximation to quantum kernel support vector regression.
result: Models with 500 training samples retain roughly 90–93% of asymptotic average precision, no severe exponential concentration is observed, and a five-landmark Nyström approximation retains 94–97% of exact-kernel performance while reducing kernel evaluations by more than 3,200-fold in one case.
conclusion: Training-set reduction and low-rank approximation can substantially lower the resources needed to train non-variational quantum kernel anomaly detectors while maintaining meaningful anomaly-discrimination performance.

title: Origin Of The Inhomogeneous Linewidth In A Solid State $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$ Nuclear Clock
authors: Kai Li, Tian Ooi, Jack F. Doyle, Konstantin Herb, Emil Pellett, Martin Pimon, Thorsten Schumm, Steven M. Girvin, Leo Radzihovsky, Jun Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Narrow linewidth (high-Q) quantum discriminators are essential for realizing solid-state [MATH]Th nuclear clocks, yet the observed transition linewidths remain at the tens-to-hundreds-of-kilohertz level, far exceeding the sub-Hertz linewidth set by the radiative lifetime of the nuclear isomer. Here, we investigate the origin of this broadening in [MATH]Th:CaF[MATH] through systematic measurements of the linewidth as functions of temperature, thorium concentration, and quadrupole state, accompanied by theoretical analysis and first-principle simulations. We find that the linewidth is independent of temperature, increases linearly with thorium concentration, and depends strongly on the quadrupole state. Data analysis identifies variations of the local electric-field gradient (EFG) as the dominant source of inhomogeneous broadening and reveals that the EFG disorder increases linearly with thorium concentration. The observed Lorentzian line shapes and linewidth linear concentration dependence are explained naturally from the [MATH] scaling of a random distribution of long-range dopant-induced perturbations. Complementary atomistic and density-functional-theory calculations reproduce these characteristic features and provide insights into the microscopic defect configurations responsible for the broadening. These results establish the dominant broadening mechanism in solid-state [MATH]Th and provide guidance for engineering nuclear-clock materials with reduced inhomogeneous broadening.
tldr: The paper identifies local electric-field-gradient disorder as the dominant source of inhomogeneous broadening in solid-state Th:CaF2 nuclear clocks, with linewidth scaling linearly with thorium concentration.
motivation: Solid-state nuclear clocks require narrow linewidths, but observed tens-to-hundreds-of-kilohertz broadening far exceeds the sub-hertz radiative limit; understanding its origin is needed to engineer better clock materials.
method: Systematic measurements of linewidth as functions of temperature, thorium concentration, and quadrupole state are combined with theoretical analysis and first-principles density-functional-theory simulations.
result: The linewidth is temperature-independent, increases linearly with thorium concentration, and depends strongly on the quadrupole state; electric-field-gradient disorder from long-range dopant-induced perturbations explains the Lorentzian lineshapes and linear concentration dependence.
conclusion: These findings establish the dominant broadening mechanism in solid-state Th:CaF2 and provide guidance for engineering nuclear-clock materials with reduced inhomogeneous broadening.

title: Quantum Sensing Applications In Consumer Electronics: Emerging Methods And Near-Term Use Cases
authors: Himanshu Thapliyal Sounak Bhowmik
abstract: ArXiv:2610.04230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum sensing is emerging as a practical means of improving sensing capabilities in consumer electronics, particularly where size, power, and noise constrain classical approaches. In this paper, we reviewed the near-term applicability of quantum sensing using a platform-and-application framework. Within this framework, we outlined the general sensing protocol and discussed the working of the four key quantum sensing platforms relevant to consumer electronics: nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, atomic vapor cells, Rydberg atomic sensors, and photonic quantum sensors. Through case studies involving navigation and positioning, healthcare and wearables, radio-frequency (RF) and wireless systems, the Internet of Things (IoT), and imaging, we examined the tangible engineering advantages offered by quantum sensing. Rather than replacing devices outright, quantum sensing is more likely to earn its place in the near-term by upgrading specific measurement components within hybrid classical-quantum systems. Right now, the clearest opportunities are in weak-field detection, compact RF reception, and sensing that remains robust in noise.
tldr: A review that surveys near-term applications of quantum sensing platforms (NV centers, atomic vapor cells, Rydberg atoms, photonic sensors) for consumer electronics such as navigation, wearables, RF reception, and IoT.
motivation: Classical sensing approaches face fundamental limits in size, power, and noise, motivating an assessment of whether quantum sensing can deliver practical improvements to consumer devices in the near term.
method: The authors use a platform-and-application framework: they outline a general sensing protocol, describe four key quantum sensing platforms, and analyze case studies in navigation/positioning, healthcare, RF/wireless, IoT, and imaging.
result: Quantum sensing is found most viable as an upgrade to specific measurement components within hybrid classical-quantum systems, with clearest near-term opportunities in weak-field detection, compact RF reception, and noise-robust sensing rather than full device replacement.
conclusion: Quantum sensing has realistic near-term niches in consumer electronics but will integrate incrementally into hybrid architectures instead of replacing classical devices outright.

title: Quaternary Preparata Codes Are Quasi-perfect Covering Codes In The Hamming Metric
authors: Tamal Maharaj
abstract: ArXiv:2610.03760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quaternary Preparata codes of Hammons, Kumar, Calderbank, Sloane and Sol\'e are [MATH]-linear codes of length [MATH] with [MATH] codewords. They are usually studied through their binary Gray images, that is, in the Lee metric. We consider them instead as codes over a 4-letter alphabet with the Hamming metric. We show that for odd [MATH] they have covering radius 2 and minimum distance 4, so they are quasi-perfect. For even [MATH] the same construction has covering radius 3. The proof is a short computation with Teichm\"uller representatives in the Galois ring [MATH], and it also gives the coset weight distribution. The covering density of these codes tends to [MATH]. The best previously known infinite families of quaternary codes with covering radius 2 have covering density about 1.5. Consequently [MATH] for all [MATH] and odd [MATH], which improves the best available bounds for a range of lengths above each [MATH]. For [MATH] the code is the octacode, and it gives [MATH]; the previous bound was 352, from 2005, and the best lower bound is 251. We also give a quaternary code showing [MATH], where the previous bound was 52, together with consequences for larger alphabets.
tldr: The paper proves that quaternary Preparata codes have covering radius 2 for odd m and 3 for even m when considered in the Hamming metric, making them quasi-perfect covering codes.
